subject: chemistry-2
question: A textbook reports a glucose concentration of 90 mg/dL and asks students to express it in mmol/L, given that the molar mass of glucose is 180 g/mol. Which sequence of conversions and result is correct?

options.text: Multiply 90 by 10 to convert dL to L, then divide by 180 to get 5 mmol/L
Multiply 90 by 180 and divide by 1000 to get 16.2 mmol/L
Divide 90 by 10 and then by 180 to get 0.05 mmol/L, since 1 L equals 10 dL
Divide 90 by 180 to get 0.5 mmol/L, since milligrams convert directly to millimoles

explanation:
One liter contains 10 deciliters, so 90 mg/dL equals 900 mg/L, and dividing by the molar mass expressed as 180 mg/mmol gives 5 mmol/L. Choice C inverts the deciliter conversion by dividing when it should multiply, which is the most frequent error here; choice D skips the volume conversion entirely. Mass-per-volume and amount-per-volume units describe the same solution, and 180 g/mol is numerically identical to 180 mg/mmol, which is what makes the second step a direct division.

ELI-10: Two independent conversions are needed, so handle them one at a time. Fix the volume first: a deciliter is one-tenth of a liter, so a liter holds ten times as much and 90 mg/dL becomes 900 mg/L. Then fix the amount unit using molar mass, which says 180 mg of glucose is one millimole, giving 900 / 180 = 5 mmol/L. Decide the direction of the volume step by asking whether a liter should contain more or less than a deciliter; the answer is more, so multiply rather than divide.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
